findings: The premise holds at this scale. In a trained 29M-parameter model, neurons are a privileged basis for LLM-named abstractions. Their strongest activations are concentrated on one gpt-6-luna token class far more than random directions' are (0.52–0.54 vs 0.29–0.41 in layers 1–3), and in the last layer on one Jev topic or format. The alignment is token-level early and topic-level late, and it emerges during training. We did not see abstractions coarsen with fewer neurons (256, 1,024 or 4,096 per layer).

Writing structure from bins works, and part of the head start lasts. A written init starts at 6.75 nats instead of 10.82. Most of that lead is spent within 10M tokens, but not all of it. Over three seeds, the written models end 0.013–0.032 nats below their same-seed baselines (seed spread 0.005), which corresponds to the baseline needing about 5–17% more tokens.

Meaning matters for passage bins, not for token bins. Bag-of-words k-means clusters of the same passages work as well as Jev's LLM bins, and shuffling the bins removes the gain, so the bins have to carry real content. At the token level, the LLM-named classes end better than distributional clusters, but random classes with the same skewed sizes do just as well. That gain comes from the one-hot class block in the embedding, not from what the classes mean. Trained neurons still align with the LLM-named classes more than with the clusters.

Left alone, the network does not use written neurons. The calibration left 171 of the 200 written neurons below threshold. ReLU² gives them no gradient, so they never wake up, and the survivors are pure but barely used: ablating all 200 costs 0.003 nats, against 0.016 for 200 ordinary neurons. Building the same construction without any neurons gives the same final loss. What helps is writing the features the neurons would read (concept evidence in the embeddings and an averaging head), not the neurons themselves.

A weight anchor preserves; a functional anchor enrols, at a price. Anchoring written weights costs almost nothing, and far less than anchoring the same entries of a random init, but the network routes around the anchored neurons. Training the neurons to predict Jev's concept makes them sharp detectors (about 52% top-1 on 160 topics) that the network uses, as the microscope shows. It costs 0.04–0.12 nats depending on strength, and only 0.01 of that is from mixing in the labelled passages. Releasing the force halfway through training keeps much of the structure for 0.03. The same force on the last layer was far worse (+0.47 to +1.05 nats), and a sharper loss made it worse still. Forcing a concept readout of the final residual stream competes directly with next-token prediction, even though the last layer is where trained models' own neurons are most topic-like.

Mechanisms are the better thing to write. The hand-built copy circuit gave the largest lasting gain in this study, and the only one that grew with scale. On the 4-layer model it ends 0.031 nats ahead after 50M tokens. On a 6-layer d=384 model trained for 100M tokens it ends 0.048 ahead (3.417 vs 3.465), roughly a quarter more effective tokens (single seed, learning rate not re-tuned). Holding the circuit in place hurts; letting training adapt it works.

What it would take to matter at scale. Writing abstractions (topic and format neurons) gave a robust but modest gain of 5–17% of training tokens, and the network did not use the written neurons themselves. Writing a mechanism the network otherwise discovers slowly gave more, and more with scale. That is the direction worth pushing toward something like nanochat: more written mechanisms (copying, previous-token and bracket tracking, n-gram memories), larger models, longer runs, and several seeds.
methods: Data. Two shards of NVIDIA ClimbMix (GPT-2 BPE tokens), shuffled by document: 548M training tokens and 4M held-out validation tokens. Every run sees the same data order unless it is a seed replicate.

Model. A 4-layer GPT (d=256, 4 heads, 1,024 ReLU² MLP neurons per layer, 29M parameters of which 26M are the untied embedding and unembedding), RoPE, parameter-free RMSNorm, document-masked causal attention over 256-token windows, zero-initialised output projections. The scale-up check uses a 6-layer d=384 version.

Training. AdamW (β = 0.9, 0.95; weight decay 0.1 on matrices), 16,384 tokens per step, 200 warmup steps, linear warm-down over the last 30%. The learning rates (4e-3 for matrices, 30× for the embedding, 3× for the unembedding) came from a 13-run sweep. Constructed and baseline models use identical hyper-parameters and, where not constructed, identical weights.

Evaluation. Validation loss on 1M held-out tokens (16 evaluations per run, plus extra early ones). Every intervention has a matched baseline with the same seed, data order and schedule. Token multipliers come from baselines trained to completion at 12.5M, 25M, 50M and 100M tokens, with log-linear interpolation. The main inits were replicated with two more seeds that change both the random init (the construction is rebuilt on it) and the data order. Controls: unigram-only, shuffled bins, random token classes, construction without neurons, anchors on a random init, and labelled-data mixing without the concept loss.

Engine. Everything was trained with a hand-written CUDA C++ trainer (SIMT kernels plus cuBLAS TF32 GEMMs, about 170k tokens/s on the RTX 3080). The forward and backward passes pass a finite-difference gradient check and match an independent NumPy implementation to 1e-4. The browser demo runs the same network from int8 weights in WebGPU (or plain JavaScript); its logits match the CPU path to 1e-5.

Abstractions and binning. gpt-6-luna proposed the taxonomy from 300 sampled passages: 160 topics in 16 groups, 40 formats, and separately 64 token classes. Jev binned 24,000 passages (20,000 for construction, 4,000 held out as probes) and the 16,000 most frequent tokens with Choice questions, which return a calibrated probability for every option. Option lists were sent as ids without descriptions to keep the cost down; on a 20-passage sample, the top label matched the described version 80% of the time for topics and 90% for formats.

Construction. Counts and linear algebra only. Token classes give a class-based bigram (one-hot class in the embedding, class-transition log-probabilities in the unembedding, in-class unigram as the output bias). Passage bins give smoothed token/concept PMI, factorised to rank 48–64, an evidence block in the embedding, a uniform-attention head, one MLP neuron per concept and its output direction. The copy circuit uses a constant residual dimension and RoPE phases to make a previous-token head, then an induction head that matches random token codes. Four to six global scales per construction were picked by grid search on held-out step-0 loss, with the same grid for every bin source.

Righting force. Weight anchor: after each AdamW step, the written weights relax toward their constructed values by min(lr·λ/rms, 1), so λ = 10 allows drift of about 10% of a tensor's typical weight. EMA variant: the anchor itself follows the weights with rate 0.002 per step. Functional anchor: 8 of the 64 sequences in each batch are Jev-labelled passages, and the 200 concept neurons' pre-activations get a softmax cross-entropy loss against Jev's distribution, per facet.
foot: Built in one session on one RTX 3080: a CUDA C++ trainer, NumPy/SciPy for the closed-form construction, Jev and gpt-6-luna for the abstractions (about $2.90 of API calls in total). Not attempted here: the text-through-images ViT variant (rendered ClimbMix pages); it is a natural next testbed, since the vision setting is where the Goodfire evidence is strongest.

Written init, no training (Jev concepts + class bigram)

copy_text: An abstraction is one kind of structure you can write; a mechanism is another. Copying is a good candidate. In about 11% of positions, the token that followed the last earlier occurrence of the current token is the next token. The baseline learns to exploit this slowly: its loss on those positions falls from 2.8 nats at 8M tokens to 0.9 at 50M, about a quarter of all its improvement in that stretch. We wrote the textbook two-head copy circuit by hand. A previous-token head attends to position t−1 using a fixed RoPE phase driven by a constant residual dimension; an induction head then matches the current token's random code against each position's previous-token code and writes the matched token's code to the output. Before any training it cuts loss on copyable positions from 5.5 to 4.3 nats. After 50M tokens it gives the best single run in this study (3.733, the baseline's loss at about 1.17× the tokens). Both models end up copying equally well; the written circuit's model is better on everything else. Holding the pattern in place with a righting force hurts, because its token codes are random vectors that the network needs to rewrite.
